facts.claim: Greater understanding of advertising did not protect against the impact of advertising on brand or product attitudes.
facts.quote: We found greater understanding did not protect against the impact of advertising on brand or product attitudes.

facts.claim: Online ('advergame') advertising combined with TV advertising causes a stronger influence on children's food consumption than TV advertising alone.
facts.quote: CONCLUSION: Online ('advergame') advertising combined with TV advertising exerted a stronger influence on children's food consumption than TV advertising alone.

facts.claim: In children exposed to unhealthy dietary marketing, dietary intake significantly increased by a mean difference [MD] = 30.4 kcal (95% confidence interval [CI] 2.9 to 57.9) during or shortly after exposure to advertisements.
facts.quote: Our meta-analysis showed that in children exposed to unhealthy dietary marketing, dietary intake significantly increased (mean difference [MD] = 30. 4 kcal, 95% confidence interval [CI] 2. 9 to 57. 9, and MD = 4. 8 g, 95%CI 0. 8 to 8. 8) during or shortly after exposure to advertisements.

facts.claim: Children exposed to food advertising on TV (11 studies) and advergames (five studies) respectively consumed an average 60.0 kcal (95% confidence interval [CI], 3.1-116.9) and 53.2 kcal (95% CI, 31.5-74.9) more than children exposed to nonfood advertising.
facts.quote: Meta-analysis revealed that children exposed to food advertising on TV (11 studies) and advergames (five studies) respectively consumed an average 60. 0 kcal (95% confidence interval [CI], 3. 1-116. 9) and 53. 2 kcal (95% CI, 31. 5-74. 9) more than children exposed to nonfood advertising.

facts.claim: Acute exposure to food advertising causes increased food intake among children and adults.
facts.quote: These findings suggest that acute exposure to food advertising increases food intake among children and adults and that the middle occipital gyrus is an implicated brain region among children.

research.angle: Food advertising causes immediate increases in calorie consumption and influences brand attitudes in children, with combined media sources having a stronger effect.
research.verdict: The evidence consistently shows that exposure to unhealthy food marketing leads to increased dietary intake and influences preferences in children.
research.caveat: Many studies were at high risk of bias, and some research focuses on acute exposure rather than long-term real-world effects.
